_note: Short site texts shown in the app. Each entry lists its reference. 'review': true marks texts written from general knowledge that the team should check before submission.

pampa-la-joya.why: Hyperarid desert in southern Peru, part of the Atacama Desert belt. Its 'Mar de Cuarzo' soils have very low organic matter, high oxidant activity and very few microorganisms: Mars-like soil properties.
pampa-la-joya.use: Test life-detection methods and instruments on Mars-like soils.
pampa-la-joya.reference: Valdivia-Silva et al. (2011), Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta. doi:10.1016/j.gca.2011.01.017

andahua.why: The 'Valley of the Volcanoes' in the Peruvian Andes: young scoria cones and lava flows at high altitude, a volcanic-terrain candidate.
andahua.use: Study volcanic morphology, surface roughness and terrain accessibility.

atacama.why: The hyperarid core of the Atacama Desert is one of the driest places on Earth, with highly saline and oxidizing soils; it has been studied as a Mars analog for about 20 years.
atacama.use: NASA has used it to test drilling and life-detection technologies for Mars.
atacama.reference: Azua-Bustos et al. (2022), Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences. doi:10.3389/fspas.2021.810426

haughton.why: An impact crater in the Canadian High Arctic (Devon Island), cold and dry, combining impact geology with a polar desert.
haughton.use: Long-running site of the NASA Haughton-Mars Project for field operations research.

makgadikgadi.why: One of the largest salt-pan systems on Earth; evaporite surfaces formed as ancient lakes dried out.
makgadikgadi.use: Compare evaporite deposits with salt-bearing terrains on Mars.
makgadikgadi.reference: Candidate listed in the team brief; reference to be added

mcmurdo.why: The McMurdo Dry Valleys are an ice-free polar desert in Antarctica, among the coldest and driest environments on Earth.
mcmurdo.use: Study cold, dry surface processes and life at the limits.
mcmurdo.reference: Candidate listed in the team brief; reference to be added

campo-piedra-pomez.why: A volcanic landscape in the Argentine Puna with Mars-analog landforms: gravel-mantled megaripples, yardangs, ventifacts and periodic bedrock ridges carved by wind.
campo-piedra-pomez.use: Study wind erosion and yardang formation comparable to Martian yardangs.

salar-pajonales.why: A calcium-sulfate salt flat in the High Andes whose climate transition partly mirrors the one proposed for early Mars.
salar-pajonales.use: Explore what the last near-surface oases for microbial life on Mars could have looked like.
salar-pajonales.reference: Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences (2022). doi:10.3389/fspas.2021.797591

iceland-highlands.why: Basaltic lava fields of the Icelandic Highlands, with fresh volcanic surfaces and little vegetation.
iceland-highlands.use: Basaltic terrain for geology training and equipment tests.
iceland-highlands.reference: Candidate listed in the team brief; reference to be added

meteor-crater.why: A well-preserved simple impact crater in the Arizona desert, the classic landform of the lunar surface.
meteor-crater.use: Used for Apollo-era astronaut geology training.

craters-of-the-moon.why: Extensive basaltic lava fields and cinder cones in Idaho.
craters-of-the-moon.use: Apollo 14 astronauts trained here in volcanic geology.

lanzarote.why: Historic basaltic eruptions (Timanfaya and Peñas de Tao). Its basalts were characterised as a lunar soil simulant comparable to Apollo 14 samples.
lanzarote.use: Lunar regolith simulant (LZS-1) for construction and resource-use tests.
lanzarote.reference: Alberquilla et al. (2022), Scientific Reports 12, 16470. doi:10.1038/s41598-022-20960-8

mauna-kea.why: High-altitude volcanic slopes with basaltic soils similar in some respects to lunar regolith.
mauna-kea.use: Testing site for lunar resource-use technologies.
